This study seeks to explore and quantify the effect of loss functions on classification performance, considering 24 diverse loss functions, accounting for confounding factors such as dataset characteristics, network configuration, and training parameters. Our investigation reveals that many notable loss functions exhibit similar performance in classification tasks, raising questions about the perceived differences in their effectiveness. Furthermore, we propose a straightforward, loss-function-independent method for determining optimal hyperparameters for stochastic gradient descent. Our study and proposed approach are conducted within the context of supervised image classification using convolutional neural networks.

This research aims to simulate thermomechanical behavior and microstructure development in polymers that crystallize under deformation. A finite element method was employed to model strain-induced crystallization, solidification, and temperature changes in polymer materials. A unique approach was developed to track crystalline phases, measuring the extent of crystallization based on mechanical properties. Experimental data from temperature increase and deformation tests were used to validate the model, and subsequent simulations were conducted to replicate tests with varying deformation rates and temperatures. The study revealed that temperature fluctuations significantly influence polymer crystallization, and an activation energy value of approximately 65700 K/kg was determined to characterize this phenomenon.

To analyze the spin-orbit coupling effects in rocksalt n-type oxides, we have developed a model that incorporates both spin-orbit coupling and lattice distortion. This model was then applied to study a particular type of iron-based superconductor, where we investigated the paramagnetic response of the Pauli susceptibility in relation to the nematic order parameter (Δm) and spin-orbit coupling (λ). Our findings showed that the influence of spin-orbit coupling can lead to a non-linear response of the Pauli susceptibility and suggested that the magnitude of the nematic order parameter could be determined by a specific magnetic field-dependent condition. Furthermore, we observed that the magnetic field behavior of the Pauli susceptibility was highly sensitive to both λ and Δm, and that the average value of the Pauli susceptibility exhibited a cubic dependence on the amplitude of the atomic vibrations (α).

In recent years, CPM has gained popularity due to its high-speed data transmission capability and low-complexity receiver design. To further improve CPM's performance in challenging environments, we focus on its resistance to delay. To this end, we examine two key factors that influence the detection performance: the length of the received data sequence and the maximum allowable delay. To enhance delay performance, we propose two receiver schemes: one with a longer data sequence length and another with a reduced allowable delay. For our proposed receiver structures, we establish conditions to ensure differential detection performance and provide delay performance benchmarks. Our results demonstrate that our proposed receiver designs can provide better delay performance while maintaining similar BER performance compared to the conventional receiver.

A previous study introduced the concept of vacuum compressibility in quantum spacetime, inversely related to quantum capacity, which measures a system's ability to encode and decode information via Gaussian processes. This study extends that work to include non-Gaussian processes and sources at finite temperature and evaluates the quantum capacity and compressibility of such sources within a Gaussian reference frame. A novel, general method for calculating the Gaussian reference frame's quantum capacity from a non-Gaussian source is developed, along with a general formula for the compressibility of sources at finite temperature. Furthermore, specific examples of sources with known temperature distributions were analyzed to illustrate the method's applicability.

In the realm of symbolic reasoning within natural language, machines have struggled to surpass human capabilities, as evident in the significant gap in accuracy between humans and machines on the ATOMIC data set. This discrepancy holds particularly true for complex conditional relationships involving multiple entities. To address this challenge, the current approach to modeling machines for this type of reasoning needs a fundamental overhaul, as simply increasing model size is no longer sufficient. In fact, current state-of-the-art models perform comparable to a simple bi-directional LSTM, which is a surprisingly basic design. To bridge the gap with human performance, future models will require more sophisticated designs that tackle the intricate patterns in natural language conditionals, as revealed by the non-trivial analysis of ATOMIC provided in this study.

This paper presents an improved method for executing the HHL algorithm on Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) devices. By creating a tailored portfolio of pseudo-operators, we minimize the overall error caused by gate execution and circuit unitary transformation. This error minimization is achieved by reducing the impact of gate errors and unitary displacement errors caused by the unitary time evolution. Our results show that for a simulated quantum device with 5 logical qubits, our method yields a 10-fold decrease in the standard deviation of execution errors compared to the original HHL algorithm. Furthermore, our approach facilitates execution of the HHL algorithm on real devices with limited qubit count, as it reduces the required qubit count by 30% relative to the original algorithm. Our research also investigates the underlying causes of execution error fluctuations and their impact on the quality of the simulation output.

To enhance data efficiency of end-to-end ASR models and facilitate practical applications, it's vital to integrate text data into the training process. This paper presents a novel approach that combines speech and text data in a multi-modal way, utilizing both encoders in a bidirectional manner to exchange semantic information. This exchange is conditioned on the forward or reverse encoding task, effectively giving different weights to the encoders' contributions. This weighted exchange enables the model to focus on either the speech or text encoding, depending on the training objective. Experimental results on the Librispeech corpus reveal a 6.15% reduction in word error rate (WER) compared to the baseline, surpassing the current state-of-the-art using only acoustic input. Additionally, this model achieves comparable performance to the current benchmark using both acoustic and phonetic inputs, demonstrating its versatility.

This paper investigates the long-term behavior of a randomly generated uniform parking distribution of size $n$, denoted as $\pi_n$. We establish that the first $k_n$ positions of $\pi_n$, $\pi_n(1)$ through $\pi_n(k_n)$, are asymptotically independent and identically distributed with a uniform probability distribution over the set $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$ for two different distance metrics. When the number of initial positions $k_n$ grows at a rate slower than $\sqrt{n}$ for the total variation distance and slower than $n$ for the Kolmogorov distance, this asymptotic behavior is shown, thereby extending previous findings by Diaconis and Hicks. Furthermore, this work also derives rate bounds and statistical limit theorems for the sum or the maximum of the first $k_n$ parking locations. Our main approach to achieving these results is by utilizing conditioned random walk reformulations.

Measurements of superconducting nanowires, particularly NbN nanowires, indicate the presence of a critical voltage threshold for dc conduction below which coherent quantum phase slips dominate, potentially blocking conduction. The exact mechanism behind this threshold behavior remains disputed. Two theories exist: one proposes it's caused by quantum phase slips within the nanowire, while the other attributes it to granular material behavior. A potential explanation for this phenomenon has been suggested by recent simulations, which demonstrate that the threshold could result from intergrain Coulomb interactions. This hypothesis is supported by the absence of threshold behavior in nanowires without strong granularity. Our research involves modifying a gate's voltage to control the threshold, and we found it could be increased by aligning the Fermi level with a particular peak in the density of states, which occurs when the electron filling fraction corresponds to an odd number. Furthermore, we observed that the threshold could be decreased by filling the peak, and in very short nanowires, the threshold disappeared altogether. A dimensionless parameter, L/lH3, which compares the mean free path length (lH) to nanowire length (L), is proposed to classify the threshold behavior based on nanowire characteristics.

Our proposed approach tackles the challenge of predicting video descriptions from unfamiliar viewpoints. We believe that both local and global features are essential for effective viewpoint-invariant representation, yet they require different treatments. To exploit their distinct characteristics, we employ a dual-learning framework, combining two separate pathways that utilize local and global features independently. Our method involves training two separate conditional generation models, one for each pathway, using a dual-learning objective that synchronizes their outputs. We evaluate our approach on the VIOLAJoint dataset and achieve state-of-the-art performance in both viewpoint-invariant representation and video prediction tasks.

In this research, we examined the interplay between coupling and level spacing using a quantum dot as a single-photon detector. By adjusting the detector's energy, we could move from a strongly coupled regime with a bound state in the continuum, through a weakly coupled regime with a quasibound state, back to a uncoupled regime with a scattering state. We measured the detector's response to a classical signal in all these regimes, confirming the interplay between coupling and level spacing. This led to a transformation from a Lorentzian to a Fano profile, offering a practical example of this phenomenon.

The Ω-baryon, which contains sss quarks and has only appeared in high-energy particle collisions since its initial discovery in 1964, has been predominantly studied using quark condensate functions and the Spectral Function, despite limited experimental data. This study compiles existing data on the masses and coupling constants of the Ω-baryon across various energy scales, employing power law and logarithmic scaling behavior. A review of past studies on the Ω-baryon's form factors is also conducted. Furthermore, this study determines the decay widths for rare processes, such as photon emission and light meson production, induced by weak electroweak forces.

Airborne transmission risk in confined environments like urban buses is intricately affected by the interaction of several factors including respiratory droplet dispersal, surface contamination, and the resulting infection among passengers and drivers. To better understand and quantify this complex dynamic, a mathematical model incorporating these elements has been developed. Subsequent modeling variations have been constructed to explore the impact of various factors on disease spread. Computational applications of these models have been used to create graphical visualizations of transmission risk zones around individuals on a bus. Notably, our results corroborate previous findings from other research, and the predictive accuracy of our model has been validated through comparison with existing data.

Recent studies indicate that spin-orbit proximity effects may appear in magnetic multilayers made of heavy elements and ferromagnetic materials. These effects could result from the interaction between a heavy element's spin-orbit interaction and the magnetic material's free spins. We used ab initio calculations to investigate the spin-orbit proximity effect in cobalt/bismuth multilayers. Our results show that even when the cobalt and bismuth layers are not adjacent, the spin-orbit proximity effect still has a notable impact on the cobalt's magnetic moments. Furthermore, we found that the magnitude of this effect decreases with increasing distance from the bismuth layers. This decline accelerates as the distance increases. Our research also identified that the magnitude of the spin-orbit proximity effect is directly related to the quantity of heavy element's interface. Consequently, increasing multilayer interface interaction can mitigate the spin-orbit proximity effect. This phenomenon can be understood by examining the cobalt's density of states at the interface. Notably, our results indicate that the spin-orbit proximity effect exhibits an oscillatory behavior due to its sensitivity to interface interaction. This behavior results in the magnetic moments varying alternately between minimum and maximum values. This oscillatory behavior could be a general feature of spin-orbit proximity effects in magnetic multilayers.

This paper provides approximate solutions to the fractional time-independent Schrödinger equation in $N$-dimensional space for a generalised Mie-type potential, expressed as $V(r^{\alpha})=A/r^{2\alpha} + B/r^{\alpha} + C$, with the aim of determining fractional quantum mechanics's effects on scattering and bound states. As the potential generalises the power, logarithmic and fractional inverse powers, our approach can tackle these cases. By employing Jumarie's fractional derivative, we transform the fractional Schrödinger equation into a solvable form, enabling us to derive the wave function and energy levels expressions. Our results also include the known cases, making them more comprehensive.

We analyze how enforcing a neural network's Lipschitz continuity, as it pertains to input sensitivity, affects its performance. In order to investigate this, we developed a straightforward approach to determine the upper bound for a neural network's Lipschitz constant, taking into consideration various $p$-norms commonly used. This approach enables us to frame training a neural network with a limited Lipschitz constant as an optimization problem that can be resolved via constrained stochastic gradient descent. Through our experiments, we found that models trained using this approach consistently performed better than those using alternative methods of regularizers. We further found that selecting hyperparameters is straightforward and demonstrated the relationship between chosen norms and the resulting model's performance. The benefits of our approach are especially apparent when neural networks are trained on limited datasets.

We've calculated the differential and total cross-sections for the production of two leptons in the Drell-Yan process within the context of third-generation gauge vector leptoquark models at the TeV scale. These calculations account for the effects of the leptoquark's interference with the standard model and were carried out using the CutTools and O'Mega programs to evaluate the cross-sections' numerical values, and the Sherpa program to simulate the events. A study of the leptoquark's contribution to the Drell-Yan cross-section revealed that it primarily comes from the $q\gamma_{Lq}$ and $\gamma_{L\ell} \ell$ vertices, and a an examination of the relevant processes' behaviors was carried out based on theoretical assumptions and loop-level calculations of the leptoquark's mass and couplings. A framework for the leptoquark's impact on the Drell-Yan cross-section was established and it was used to create the code for calculating the cross-sections at the LHC run 3 and a future pp collider with 100 TeV.

Radiation exposure during positron emission tomography (PET) scans restricts their usage for sensitive groups, such as pregnant women and young individuals requiring frequent imaging, due to compromised image quality from lower doses or shortened scan times. Deep-learning models have made significant advancements in enhancing PET images by translating low-quality PET scans with associated MRI data to higher-quality PET images, particularly with significantly reduced doses. Nonetheless, such deep learning approaches have been primarily focused on utilizing training datasets similar to their test data, neglecting performance evaluation for new acquisitions outside of their distribution. We developed a novel neural network framework that incorporates the physics underlying the PET imaging process and estimates output uncertainty to address these limitations. This new uncertainty-aware neural network framework can utilize low-dose PET scans and accompanying MRI data to generate high-quality PET images at standard doses, thereby enhancing image information and reducing estimated output uncertainty. Experiments conducted on low-dose PET scans with corresponding MRI data demonstrated that this novel approach yields images of higher quality, both quantitatively and qualitatively, in comparison to existing deep learning models. Furthermore, evaluations of normal operational conditions and outside-the-distribution scenarios showed that this new method performs well, even with new acquisitions outside of their distribution.

We analyze the relationship between centering theory and coreference resolution using modern neural approaches. Centering theory, an information-flow model, describes how discourse entities are drawn from world knowledge. This study investigates if current coreference systems, trained on standard data sets, adequately capture centering principles. Our results show that these systems, despite achieving high accuracy, exhibit significant flaws in relation to centering. Specifically, we found that they fail to demonstrate a clear understanding of the concept of "focus" and how it relates to new and given information. Furthermore, we observed a discrepancy between how entities are labeled as "new" or "given" and how coreference systems resolve them. Our data also suggests that centering principles are not consistently applied across all instances of coreference. We attribute this inconsistency to the prevalence of entity-rhetoric pairs overwhelming the influence of centering. Our findings are consistent across two diverse coreference systems, demonstrating that there is room for improvement in neural approaches to coreference resolution.

In critical applications like emergency response systems and sporting events, accurate player positioning is vital. Traditional methods use triangulation techniques with high precision access points, but installing such devices in many situations is impractical due to their cost and the difficulty of mounting them. This study investigates the potential of using existing routers already present in an environment to estimate a person's location using their WiFi signal strength. A novel approach is proposed that leverages a custom dataset to train a predictive model, which estimates the person's location within the environment. The proposed method is tested using both simulated data and real-world WiFi signals from an outdoor environment, and the results show that it can accurately determine a person's location across various scenarios.

This study examines how beam bunch train interactions affect beam stability in energy recovery linacs that use recirculating accelerators. By analyzing beam breakup instability, this research aims to provide guidelines for optimal filling patterns to ensure reliable operation. Computational simulations were conducted to evaluate several filling designs, with different beam bunch spacings serving as variables. The results show that, to prevent beam breakup instability, there is a minimum spacing required between beam bunches, which is dependent on both beam charge and machine parameters. Furthermore, this threshold distance must be exceeded to prevent instability, and excessive spacing will simply waste productivity resources. The studies were conducted using a real-machine model incorporating magnetic fields and particle dynamics, yielding accurate and applicable predictions.

To extend the BFKL equation to NNLL accuracy, the one-loop CEV for two gluons with low rapidity ordering must be known. In this work, the dispersive part of a one-loop six-gluon amplitude in N=4 SYM theory was calculated under a NMRK kinematic limit and shown to be composed of a two-gluon CEV, allowing extraction of the latter for all helicity configurations. Although this calculation was constrained to the NMRK limit, the resulting two-gluon CEV exhibits significant complexity in both color and kinematic dependence, mirroring characteristics found in general six-gluon amplitude configurations. As such, this two-gluon CEV can be viewed as representative of general six-gluon amplitude characteristics, valid beyond the NMRK limit.

Theories explaining highly extended, molten polymer brush properties have provided valuable insights into the behavior of surface-grafted polymers. However, these models typically require the absence of obstacles or inclusions within the brush, limiting their applicability to controlled laboratory settings. In contrast to these scenarios, we examine strongly stretched, molten brushes attached to an interface that includes non-polymeric inclusions filled with good or poor solvents. Our analysis shows that although these inclusions disrupt the brush's uniformity, they do not affect the brush's overall extent when the inclusions are fully embedded within the interface. Furthermore, our research demonstrates that the brush's thickness can be distinguished from the inclusions' characteristics, enabling the determination of the brush's thickness, inclusions' shape, and the exponent that governs its scaling just by observing the brush's overall extent in various directions. In the case of spherical inclusions, our model predicts a specific exponent of 2.36, independent of the inclusions' size. Our theoretical approach is complemented by simulations that confirm our findings and demonstrate the impact of brush incompatibility within the inclusions' volume.

A graph G is said to have metric dimension d if there are d vertices whose encoding vector is the identity, meaning that any two distinct vertices have distinct encoded values. This concept originated in physics to identify state spaces in particle detection problems and has since been applied in biology, chemistry, and physics. However, this condition requires every pair of vertices to have a distinct encoded value, which can be extremely rare and often there are constraints on the available vertices that can be used for this purpose. To accommodate this, we introduce a new parameter, the d-dimensional trimmed metric dimension, which is defined as the smallest number t such that removing at most n-t vertices yields a subgraph with a metric dimension d. We prove several properties of this new parameter, including it being least when the remaining vertices form a d-fold identity, which we use as a starting point to establish upper and lower bounds for t. Specifically, we find that for d=2, t is equal to the second smallest of the maximum degree, the girth number squared, (dimension of the identity matrix d)x(n), and the number of vertices n. For general d, we show that the smallest of the max degree, the girth number squared, (d x n), and n must satisfy t ≥ n/(d+1), which we further refine to n/(d+2) when the graph is regular. We also explore a more constrained version, the localized version, and determine its value for specific graphs and

Researchers have applied various techniques using machine learning and image analysis to enhance all-sky maps made from the Fermi Large Area Telescope's data, particularly in identifying variable sources. By utilizing a simple model, a map enhancement method was developed to concentrate on sources with significant intensity fluctuations, thus supplementing existing catalogs. This technique's effectiveness was demonstrated by reprocessing known variable sources and discovering additional sources with gamma-ray emission variability, highlighting the potential of this approach for handling large data sets.

In large-scale network optimization tasks, having an automated decision-making process for individual nodes can be beneficial. For example, in wireless communication networks, optimizing signal transmission can improve performance. Another example involves balancing energy consumption in distributed computing systems. To address these challenges, we introduce the concept of network monarchies, which are comprised of individual decision-making units, sorted in a hierarchical order based on their importance. We then focus on optimizing over a specific type of network monarchy, called a serial monarchy, and provide a mathematical framework including dynamic programming and linear programming components. To demonstrate the practical applications of this framework, we perform simulations using a model of a wireless communication network.

This paper describes a method for locating binary asteroid candidates within Pan-STARRS1 images based on their orbital patterns, and outlines a statistical approach to evaluate the detection probability of these objects within the described scenarios. A simulation of the detection process yielded a log-normal distribution of detectable $a_1$ values, with an average of 0.25 AU and a standard deviation of 0.09, indicating that only a small fraction of binary asteroids with closely spaced trajectories will be uncovered. A scan through known asteroids ended up flagging three asteroids with known binary companions, along with potential candidates 288R and 162R, although verification of these discoveries will depend on additional observations.

This study examines a partially linear regression model where the outcome variable forms a network with other observed variables, and we find that model specifications can be identified under certain conditions. Furthermore, we establish that, under specific moment conditions, the model parameters can be estimated at a rate that scales with the sample size, allowing for valid inferences. A GMM estimation approach for model parameters is proposed and we establish the asymptotic normality of estimators derived from a continuous weighting function. To validate our findings, we conduct a simulation study. Notably, we apply this analysis to investigate peer effects within a network context using data from the Add Health study.

This study introduces novel fractional integral and derivative operators based on the Riemann-Liouville variable-order fractional calculus, and derives a modified Leibniz rule for these operators. Notably, a modified version of the Taylor series expansion is also established.

We introduce the G4C challenge, focusing on how natural language interactions can be guided by set objectives, which can be evaluated through role-playing games like Dungeons and Dragons. Two critical components are identified that are essential for effective player-guidance: understanding the player's intentions and ability to reason about the player's mental state. Without loss of generality, we assume that intentions are known, and focus on developing a theory-of-mind capability. This is achieved by proposing a novel approach that combines conversational knowledge with mental state reasoning, leveraging conversational knowledge to drive theory-of-mind, which is a novel strategy. Our method comprises multiple components, primarily drawing from conversational knowledge, combined with separate modules for intent recognition, intent selection, and theory-of-mind reasoning. Evaluations using Dungeons and Dragons as our test bed show that this approach yields superior results compared to existing challenges, alongside significant improvements in areas such as response diversity and player engagement.

Proteins exert their functions through the precise arrangement of their polypeptide chains, and the relationship between their 3D structure and flexibility is closely tied to these functions. proteins containing knotted structures pose a significant challenge for protein dynamics and function, as unknotting processes would divert energy and resources away from vital cellular processes. Yet, knotted proteins exist in nature, suggesting their structures can be highly stable and resistant to knot unwinding. a new statistical approach, inspired by topological ideas, allows for the identification of unknotting pathways on a protein's surface by analyzing 3D structures. this method reveals that knotted proteins with twisted structures tend to have limited unknotting pathway options, whereas proteins with looped structures have more pathway choices. this distinction highlights the importance of protein topology in determining their flexibility andunknotting processes. furthermore, by classifying knotted proteins based on their unknotting pathways and comparing them to random knot structures, an interesting phenomenon is observed: the unknotting pathways of real proteins tend to avoid certain surface regions, specifically near hydrophobic residues. this preference is not seen in random knot structures, suggesting that surface knotting interactions play a significant role in shaping the unknotting processes of real proteins. this phenomenon's underlying causes could be related to protein functions, evolution, and stability.

Let $\omega$ be a symplectic form on the real $4$-dimensional torus $T^4$, and define the symplectic mapping category group of $T^4$ with respect to $\omega$ as the set of diffeomorphisms $f: (T^4,\omega) \to (T^4,\omega)$ that maintain the contact structure, up to isomorphism. These groups will be denoted as $\text{SC}_\omega(T^4)$. Given that $9$ generators form a basis for $\text{SC}_\omega(T^4)$, further investigation is necessary to determine if there exists a specific real number $\kappa$ for which $\text{SC}_\omega(T^4)$ can be consistently described using the basis $\{[z_i]: i=1,...,9\} \cup \{[\phi_j]: j=9,...,16\}$ and the relation $[\phi_j](z_i)=e^{\pi i \kappa/2}z_i$ for $1 \leq i \leq 9$ and $9 \leq j \leq 16$.

A detailed investigation of the conventional NG theorem is presented, with a
subsequent focus on a model featuring a massless scalar field coupled to a
next-generation Dirac fermion within both relativistic QFT and quantum many-
body theories. The analysis involves constructing a suitable vacuum state, as
well as general quasiparticle descriptions for the scalar and fermionic fields.
The usual NG theorem is demonstrated to not hold in either context, with the
scalar excitations displaying an anomalous mass term directly resulting from
the breakdown of symmetry. Additionally, an examination of the usual NG
behavior is performed for both a massless scalar field in quantum many-body
systems and the long-wavelength limit of a Bose-Einstein condensate. A
related, more general discussion on the characteristics of quasiparticles within
symmetry-broken states is also presented.

Our proposed method, dubbed Generative Counterfactual Sentence Modification (GCSM), aims to modify specific aspects of sentences. However, implementing GCSM requires a strong language model, easy input/output specifications, and a scoring function to evaluate revised sentences. We employ a reinforcement learning approach using easy input/output specifications and positive samples as guides, with the strength of our language model as the evaluation criterion. Consequently, we can generate high-quality counterfactual sentences. To demonstrate the versatility of this strong model, we partake in the task of modifying the second person to the first person in sentences, although this study primarily focuses on GCSM. We have made GCSM available for public use.

Research into remote epitaxy on monolayer graphene is hindered by the unknown interaction between graphene and growing films. This study investigates Co2FeAl Heusler films deposited on graphene and sapphire substrates using in situ X-ray techniques during growth, and postgrowth analysis via scanning tunneling microscopy and X-ray absorption fine structure. When deposited directly on sapphire, these films exhibit a faceted crystal structure with pinhole-free surfaces due to the remote epitaxial growth mechanism. In contrast, films deposited on graphene show a square-shaped crystal structure and larger grain sizes, potentially resulting from van der Waals epitaxy. The remote epitaxial growth mechanism is confirmed by minimizing misfit dislocations, while the square-shaped crystal structure's explanation lies in the almost equilateral lattice parameter mismatch between Heusler and graphene. The lack of faceted crystal structures on graphene can be attributed to the effects of Co segregation and oxygen exposure. This study demonstrates control over Heusler films' crystal structure, from faceted through square to cubic shapes, by adjusting Co content and oxygen exposure. These findings are significant for developing remote epitaxy on monolayer graphene and for understanding Heusler films' magnetic properties, as they are unaffected by the film's crystal structure.

A code is referred to as $ \Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear if it results from a particular type of encoding process called the Gray image of a code that has properties derived from $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-additive code, given a prime number p greater than two. This paper specifically delves into the examination of the dimension of the kernel of a map associated with these $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-additive codes and aims to provide an explicit formula for this dimension in a specific context.

In the task of identifying categories for objects within images, models are often given object masks instead of full category labels. This makes it easier to provide annotations, as it requires less expertise and can be obtained from existing segmentation datasets. However, working with partial annotations poses a significant challenge when it comes to evaluating models. Ideally, the assigned mask should correspond to only one object within the image, yet such carefully created annotations do not generally exist. In fact, research has shown that most annotated datasets do not meet this criterion, according to an examination of five notable datasets, including MISC, PASCAL VOC, NWPU, DOTA, and COCO. To address this issue, a new annotation protocol is proposed which involves creating multi-label samples from single positive labels. In this approach, an object mask that represents multiple objects within an image is considered a single positive label, indicating that models can still leverage existing datasets despite not being perfectly clean. This new protocol is tested on a dataset that contains only single positive labels and yields promising results, according to evaluation metrics.

The GNS construction links any pair consisting of a unital algebra and a state that maps unitals to the unit, to a unique pair made up of a Hilbert space and a unitary representation of the algebra's inverse to its dual algebra. We demonstrate that the GNS construction acts as a two-sided inverse to the process of creating a state, first taking a unital algebra, taking its dual, reversing the representation, before finally obtaining the original state. We achieve this by incorporating the GNS construction within a process known as composition, and another process known as evaluation. Both processes are defined in a way that the GNS construction, combined with its dual, results in the original state. We validate our understanding by verifying that the process of creating a state from a unital algebra, combined with the process of obtaining a unital algebra from a state, results in the original unital algebra. We also establish that the process of creating a state from a unital algebra, combined with the process of obtaining a unital algebra from a state, is equivalent to the process of creating a state from the unital algebra formed by obtaining a unital algebra from a state. We utilize this characterization to identify unital algebras that are invariant under the process of creating a state and being returned to the original state.

The emergence of gamma-ray telescopes has allowed for a deeper understanding of the cosmic spectrum, but the origins of its highest energy component remain unclear. We propose a source for gamma-rays in certain galaxies with tightly wound magnetic fields, where accelerated particles typically miss their central black hole. Utilizing accurate calculations of magnetic field lines, we model the movement of charged particles to determine the likelihood of missing the black hole's accretion disk. A an analytical formula is then used to estimate this probability, which is crucial for determining the energy of gamma-rays produced by particle collisions. A simulation of 19 galaxies with closely wound magnetic fields reveals that all low-power galaxies lack gamma-rays, whereas the most powerful ones emit gamma-rays primarily above their black holes. An analytical formula is derived to describe this behavior, which is then used to predict the gamma-ray energy of galaxies like NGC 4382 and NGC 4517. These calculations can be used in a broader context to understand the relationship between galaxies' gamma-ray energy and their magnetic field properties.

This study involves modeling heart sound samples that contain noise and distorted recordings to aid in developing robust machine learning algorithms for heart sound diagnosis. A total of 150 recordings from the PhysioNet database were used to create 150 training examples and 50 test examples, each representing a third-dimensional feature space of heart sound patterns. These examples account for both temporal and frequency domain characteristics and were tested using three different classification techniques. The results show that decision-boundary-based methods such as support vectors and linear discriminant analysis outperformed the k-nearest neighbors algorithm. Additionally, the study found that both support vectors and linear discriminant analysis performed equally well, with an accuracy of 0.85 in the low-noise condition, but with a notable difference in processing time.

The proliferation of computing technology and wearable devices like smartphones and wristbands allows users to easily access health information and conduct various physical activities anywhere, at any time. However, the disparity in data quality affects model performance, as it is typically trained on data from a small number of healthy users with extensive activity histories. To address this challenge, we propose FedHealth, a pioneering federated transfer knowledge framework for wearable healthcare. FedHealth leverages cloud storage to share data and models among participants, enabling model transfer without exchanging raw data. It incorporates a hybrid scheme that combines federated training and transfer learning to enhance model performance. Furthermore, FedHealth can handle an unlimited number of participants with varying data amounts, reducing privacy and storage risks. Experimental evaluations using real-world data from users with different activity levels demonstrate the effectiveness of FedHealth.

This study classifies portfolio optimization strategies with higher order moments including skewness and kurtosis to aid Hedge Fund practitioners in navigating various paradigms and methodologies. Key research approaches, such as utility theory and multi-objective optimization, are reviewed, with an examination of their benefits and limitations.

The rising complexity of software systems of varying kinds, coupled with
the necessity for nearly instantaneous results, demands significant automation
in the field of software processing. Multiple factors are contributing to this
complexity: the enormous scale of modern software, its multi-faceted nature,
and the varied contexts in which it's used. This workshop will delve into the
latest innovations and challenging issues in the development of automated
technologies for processing intricate, complex software systems. It will feature
an examination of the current state of the art, as well as the potential future
directions in this field, following on from the successful workshops held in
2019 and 2020.

This study examines a complex control problem characterized by multiple stochastic price paths whose depths can change suddenly. The problem aims to minimize expected future costs under these dynamic conditions. A key finding demonstrates that, when there are no upper bounds on the size of price jumps, a solution may not always exist for this control issue. Conversely, when upper limits do exist, a solution can be found for problems with finite costs. The research also explores links to similar problems with unbounded price movements. A sample model with programmable temperature regulation is presented as a specific application of this control concept.

To explore the significance of even and odd leptoquark pair production at the Large Hadron Collider, even leptoquarks with charge 5/3 are considered, specifically assuming a consistent theoretical framework that includes both even (LQ~T3) and odd (LQ~T2) types and examining the impact of uneven production processes on the (T3 LQ~) (T3 LQ~) pair production process, it has been found that even leptoquark pair production dominates and the number of even leptoquark pairs produced is greater than the number of odd leptoquark pairs produced, furthermore, uneven production processes delay the point of equal abundance by 5 to 30 TeV, also, even leptoquark pair production processes have uneven distributions of quark and lepton flavors systems, even leptoquark pair production processes dominate rare charged meson generation and heavy neutrino generation processes, even leptoquarks with a mass of 1000 TeV require strong coupling constants greater than 1.1 times the weak coupling constant.

We analyzed a sample of 106 galaxies for which data is available for two fine structure lines of neutral carbon, and we found that the line ratio deviates from the expected equilibrium value in 24 galaxies, likely due to a non-LTE condition. By modeling the line ratio, we distinguished between two scenarios: a non-LTE condition caused by a strong external UV field or a low carbon density, and we found that a low carbon density is more common. A low gas phase carbon density is rare in galaxies but has been observed in dwarf galaxies and starburst galaxies. It tends to decrease the column density of molecular gas but increase the gas phase oxygen abundance, which has been confirmed using another method. This effect is more significant at lower stellar masses. Notably, a low carbon density is more prevalent in galaxies with very low extreme infrared-ratio, indicating a lack of hot dust, and it also correlates with the line ratios of other molecules, specifically CO and HCN, which can be a valuable indicator for researchers studying these molecules in low-carbon-density environments.

In 2004, Zhang introduced the sequence reconstruction model where an attacker seeks to replicate a random sequence from a set of identical-looking sequences based on a subset of observed sequences. This model incorporates various distance metrics to determine how difficult it is for an attacker to recreate the original sequence. Our study examines the average number of observed sequences required to accurately identify the original sequence using the Hamming distance metric and presents statistical tables for different types of original sequences and observed sequence sets. Notably, we discovered that the attacker's ability to recreate the original sequence is directly influenced by its size, and a simple formula can be derived to calculate the average number of observed sequences needed to replicate the original sequence with a certain level of accuracy.

Researchers anticipate that Pulsar Timing Array (PTA) experiments will be capable of detecting gravitational waves produced by individual supermassive black hole binaries moving in highly elliptical orbits. By comparing various methods for computing PTA signals from these binaries, our findings indicate that employing approximate analytic expressions yields the most efficient computation, leading to a significant reduction of up to 50 times in computational costs compared to other methods. The accuracy of these analytic expressions is validated through a relevant mismatch metric and found to be sufficiently precise for the PTA parameter space of interest. Furthermore, we introduce an improved approach using spline interpolation to enhance the computation speed for specific narrow-band PTA datasets. The implementation of these findings in the GWecc package enables seamless access to our analytic expressions and spline data via the PySTISE interface, facilitating easy adoption into existing PTA data analysis pipelines.

We present a novel stochastic velocity model, inspired by ASEP dynamics, where the speed of each particle is drawn from a uniform distribution within a given range. We determine the hydrodynamic limits of both local and global ASEP velocity processes, obtaining specific mean-field and non-linear equations governing the system's evolution. The study of the global model leads to a new class of hydrodynamic equations, while the local model yields a system identical to the one obtained from the hydrodynamic limit of the TASEP process. The study also includes a discussion on the condition ensuring system stability.

This study examines various mathematical models developed in response to the ongoing pandemic to address pressing issues affecting public health policy and understanding of epidemic dynamics. Beginning with an overview of fundamental Kermack-McKendrick model characteristics, we delve into generalized models, considering applications such as network structures, simultaneous transmission of viruses, the patterns of epidemic curve growth, probability distributions, and critical time periods for model compartment analysis. A unified framework emerges, emphasizing the critical role that context, drawing from epidemiology, medicine, and biology, plays in informing both model development and analysis. Failing to consider the biological implications of mathematical models during data fitting risks producing statistically significant results, but lacking practical significance for guiding pandemic management, mitigation, and eventual control.

Researchers who work with ultracold atoms and molecules have access to a wide range of theoretical possibilities due to the precise control they can exercise over interactions and spin states. A key aspect is the interplay between spin symmetry and interactions, specifically in the case of two-component systems with contact interactions. These interactions can either support spin symmetry or break it, resulting in competing effects on atom-molecule conversion processes. A key finding from theoretical simulations highlights the benefits of using a specific three-body recombination channel that forms a molecule with spin symmetry, compared to others that do not, as it reduces the energy required to create a molecule from two identical spin-aligned atoms. This result is particularly significant for systems with two hyperfine levels, and it was found that a particular two-photon process can influence this scenario, either maintaining spin symmetry forever, altering the necessary energy, or even changing the required conditions for it. Notably, this particular two-photon process can result in a specific three-body recombination channel that forms a molecule with antiparallel spins from two identical spin-aligned atoms, a phenomenon that has never been observed before, and it requires a specific atomic species that has two accessible hyperfine levels. This phenomenon is associated with a frequency range that is determined by the difference between two specific atomic energy levels, and it can result in either destructive interference with atom-molecule conversion processes or, alternatively, a significant enhancement of them, depending on the specific conditions.

Our proposed DNA-storage system builds upon the base provided by previous technology, enhancing it to efficiently manage complex data structures, including binary trees, and facilitating easy updates to stored data. To accomplish this, we developed a custom encoding method that transforms binary tree nodes into a suitable format for storage. Furthermore, we created a command set for managing data updates. In experiments, we found our technology excels in managing and updating binary tree-based data, outperforming the base standard specified in [13] by up to 6-fold for data updates.

Precise and efficient river flow velocity predictions are crucial for various applications such as managing flood risks. While the shallow water equations are commonly employed for this purpose, their traditional numerical solutions can be time-consuming and require sophisticated technical expertise. In contrast, the proposed method utilizes a two-layer neural network to directly estimate river flow velocity observations at specific points. This approach allows for rapid velocity predictions without the need for extensive computational resources or complex mathematical knowledge. A field trial in Japan demonstrated the efficacy of this method in predicting flow velocities similar to those obtained from the Mikami et al. solver, a well-regarded solution to the shallow water equations.

HDR photography combines multiple photos captured at various exposure levels to correct overexposed or underexposed areas in an image. This research presents a novel approach to automatically produce HDR images using only a single smartphone camera, without the need for additional images. A new technique, called histogram-based fusion, is introduced to merge two images with distinct exposure settings. This method determines the optimal image fusion point based on the histogram analysis of captured photos, ensuring that only areas outside the 75% brightness range are combined, thereby preventing unnatural color discrepancies. The proposed technique was tested and compared to existing HDR creation methods, demonstrating improved outcomes in terms of visual appeal, color accuracy, and overall performance.

Causal deep learning is a rapidly evolving field that is heavily influenced by new data sets and machine learning models. This field, which was first introduced in 2012, has experienced significant growth over the past decade, with over 2,500 published research papers. Our comprehensive review of the field's development includes an in-depth analysis of its underlying principles, as well as the methods and tools used in the field. We also examine the empirical studies conducted within the field and the broader implications of its findings. Our goal in creating this review is to provide a clear understanding of the field's current state, its potential applications, as well as the challenges it faces. We conclude by identifying promising research directions and areas worthy of further exploration.

This note presents a new category of map functions known as oriented colored broken submersions, which forms a more comprehensive class that encompasses both colored and oriented map functions. We demonstrate that any map that falls into this broader category is topologically equivalent to a map that can be refined to a submersive map whose differential has a full rank. This in-depth analysis is a direct consequence of the recent proof of the extended Alexander-Pontryagin theorem, which also implies that being treatable is equivalent to being approximable through maps that are part of the more inclusive oriented colored broken submersions category.

This study compares the efficiency of Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) and Algebraic Multigrid (AMG) methods for solving complex cardiac mechanics problems on various high-performance computing architectures. The heart model involves nonlinear mechanical models, electrical activation influencing mechanical activity, and ion channel populations, requiring both iterative and direct solution approaches. Solving one second-step linear system from the Newton iteration requires between 2,500 to 17,000 seconds for the BDDC and between 560 to 3,800 seconds for the AMG solutions, depending on the specific geometry. Further, the BDDC solution times increase more significantly than the AMG solution times as problem size increases, although both solutions scale suboptimally with better times for smaller problems. The research highlights notable variations in solution times across different architectures for both the direct and iterative solutions, as well as the influence of Lagrange multipliers and subdomain sizes on the BDDC solution time.

Standard diffusion models can fail, particularly when influenced by correlations and variations, where mean squared displacements grow in a linear manner with time. We investigate the spread of a fractional Brownian population exhibiting time-dependent and diverse diffusion characteristics. Our primary objective is to establish the relationship between these individual characteristics and the population's spatial distribution as observed over time. We examine the applicability and limitations of this approach to a broad category of self-similar diffusion processes, utilizing a general framework that is subsequently applied to recognized processes such as Laplace diffusion, nonlinear diffusion, and their variants.

A fundamental theory is developed to describe both linear and Kerr nonlinear interactions between the modes of dielectric optical resonators, with the framework being applicable across various geometries and modes. The general approach allows for a straightforward computation of linear mode interactions, and the dimensionless form of the exact linear interaction matrix is validated through numerical simulations. Furthermore, the theory is applied to a ring resonator with a microring coupled to it, and the results are compared to existing studies. The effects of mode similarity and mode phase mismatch are quantified in the dimensionless cross-phase modulation and four-wave mixing coefficients. The theory is subsequently extended to a waveguide with a long straight section, and the computation of mode interactions and nonlinear interactions is carried out. The developed approach is demonstrated to provide accurate predictions of linear mode interactions and the results are compared to existing empirical models of nonlinear interactions. The theory is expected to be a useful tool for designing optical devices based on mode interactions and nonlinear effects in resonators and waveguides.

A convolutional neural network technique has been successfully applied to generate highly detailed, high-resolution images from low-resolution sensors measuring turbulent fluid dynamics. A separate convolutional neural network was utilized for high-resolution image analysis, and a generative adversarial network was employed to train the two models to accurately replicate high-resolution images from low-resolution data. A separate training session was conducted for each of the three high-resolution image analyses. A model specifically designed to predict specific high-resolution image aspects was then developed and trained. This model was then used to generate high-resolution images from low-resolution data in various Reynolds number scenarios. Notably, the technique was tested on a flow with built-in obstacles, demonstrating its practical applicability.

For most real-world tasks, successful applications of reinforcement learning depend heavily on multiple related tasks being learned simultaneously. In contrast, widely used evaluation methods, including the standard suite of Suite of Reinforcement Learning Benchmarks, focus primarily on individual learning tasks. As a result, there is a lack of publicly available data to measure the performance of reinforcement learning models across changing problem domains. To address this critical issue, we've created L2Explorer, a cutting-edge evaluation platform that systematically challenges reinforcement learning models through progressively introduced new and varying learning objectives. In L2Explorer, tasks are introduced or removed from an ever-expanding set of 20 underlying tasks, each drawn from six distinct domains. By designing this dynamic environment, we identify and report several notable findings: (1) the importance of selecting relevant tasks is stressed, as failing to do so can significantly lower performance; (2) constant learning leads to improved results, whereas task removal leads to performance decline; (3) domain-specific knowledge persists even after the associated task is removed; (4) L2Explorer differentiates between long-term learning challenges, such as slow performance improvement, and short-term difficulties, like sudden drops in performance. To facilitate reproducibility, our research includes three accompanying algorithms: (1) a baseline constant-learning model; (2) an enhanced model that produces domain-specific future tasks; and (3) a more intricate model that consistently learns new tasks while dropping unnecessary ones. All associated code and data are publicly available for further

In dynamic environments, where declarative processes are used to great effect, due to their flexibility, there is a growing need to balance process adaptation with the risk of unintended consequences. To safely alter a process, one must consider not only what actions are permitted by the process definition, but also the potential effects of those actions on the process's objectives. In this paper, we introduce a method for declarative process exploration that takes into account the potential impact of actions on the process's goals, providing a set of safe actions that can be executed to achieve desired outcomes. We have implemented this method in the context of dynamic declarative processes, and tested its efficacy under various scenarios.

This study focuses on extending certain algebraic and analytic properties from input spaces to modulation spaces, specifically focusing on closed subsets within the real plane and closed subsets within the complex plane. Some notable results include proving that when the input space allows Descent via Geometric Rationality, the moduli space will also allow this property in the context of algebraic properties. Conversely, having this property in the moduli space does not necessarily imply it in the input space, although it does hold when the input space enables analytic properties. Additionally, extending analytic properties such as compactness or quasicompactness from the input space to the moduli space is also explored, along with examining how these properties interact with morphisms and closed maps.

The link between galactic nuclei and star-forming regions at the heart of galaxies has long been observed and closely examined. A potential imbalance in mass accretion flow in black hole systems residing in massive galaxies has been proposed as an explanation for the observed relationship between supermassive black holes and their surrounding stars. However, the underlying causes for the observed relationship between mass and star formation rate in galaxies remain unclear, with model predictions suggesting a distinct turn in the relationship's slope for the most massive galaxies. A study of 176 optically bright active galactic nuclei, incorporating spectral energy distributions to determine total infrared radiation and accurate measurements of nuclear stellar mass, reveals that the mass accretion flow in these systems is indeed sufficient to explain the relationship between mass and star formation rate, with irradiation from the central source contributing significantly to the total infrared radiation. Furthermore, by accounting for dust heating sources, the study finds that the majority of infrared radiation in these systems originates from stellar mass rather than direct thermal emission from the accretion disk. A new scaling relation that considers the ratio of mass accretion flow to nuclear stellar mass provides valuable insights into the physics governing these systems, with results showing that approximately half of the available radiation is generated through the low-radius, optically thick accretion flow in the nuclear region.

This study conducts sentiment analysis across languages, examining the
emotional content of news articles using both few-shot and zero-shot learning
techniques. The primary objective is to categorize news articles as expressing
positive, negative, or neutral sentiment, using only the abstract text. A total
of 6,000 abstracts were collected from Polish, with corresponding English
sentiment classifications. The document abstracts were labeled as expressing positive
or negative sentiment in the native language. The underlying language was
switched from Polish to English, repeating the process described above. The
sentiment analysis was performed using both BERT and our proposed multi-task
model. The evaluation showed that the proposed model consistently outperformed
the BERT baseline for both languages. The model performed particularly well in
the zero-shot setting, with the F1-score for Polish being 0.378 and for
English 0.402. The research also examined the importance of using the native
language for training, switching languages, and the quantity of training
data.

X-ray images contain rich information that can be used for both medical diagnosis and patient management decisions involving COVID-19 patients admitted to intensive care units. However, the automated analysis of these images lags behind their manual analysis. To bridge this gap, an automatic method is proposed to extract relevant features from images using convolutional neural networks. The proposed method leverages a pre-trained VGG16 network to generate intermediate attributes that can be used to classify images. New attributes are then derived from these classifications, which can be utilized in machine learning models to predict patient outcomes. The proposed method was tested using a synthetic dataset composed of real data from two separate institutions. The results showed that the features obtained from images can predict patient outcomes with moderate accuracy. Furthermore, the attributes extracted from images can be used to train a classifier on a limited sample size, which can then be used to extend the prediction to new patients. The proposed method provides a foundation for using deep learning on small datasets of ICU patients with COVID-19.

The notion of a collection in category theory has been equivalently defined as either a family of objects and morphisms satisfying certain properties or, alternatively, a single object whose endomorphisms form a free monoid. Building upon the concept of symmetric operations initially introduced by J.R. Kelsishan, we demonstrate that the latter perspective can be represented using simplicial objects, specifically a simplicial group. Furthermore, we establish a connection between this construction and the simplicial operators defined by Makkai and Reyes.

This paper delves into the source of a major challenge in VRD tasks, namely the extensive number of spurious relationships discovered. We contend that the primary issue lies in models incorrectly associating background information with common common objects. To address this, we propose a novel spatial attention mechanism that guides the model to focus on object interactions within the image, rather than the entire image. Furthermore, we introduce a novel category attention mechanism that causes the model to focus on specific object categories involved in relationships. Both of these mechanisms were implemented as part of a multi-task framework, combining VRD with object classification. Our approach demonstrates notable improvements in detection accuracy, with the spatial attention mechanism contributing a 4.5% absolute improvement and the category attention mechanism a 5.3% absolute improvement in the VRE-CAP dataset.

We've performed an in-depth analysis of three galaxy cores at $\rm z=2.91$ within a massive galaxy group, yielding high-resolution infrared and submillimeter data. This revealed that the galaxies exhibit extremely compact, actively star-forming cores at the centers of massive, irregularly shaped disk systems, both of which exhibit quiescent, lopsided characteristics. Consequently, these galaxies are witnessing `outside-in' quenching. We estimate the galaxies have maintained their accretion rates and possess disks with masses similar to low-$\rm z$ galaxies. Nevertheless, they exhibit enhanced bulge formation, counter to the prevailing outside-in quenching paradigm. This phenomenon is attributed to the sustained impact of gas streams that are causing accretion, fueling both star formation and disk asymmetry, ultimately contributing to the development of bulges. Furthermore, we propose that these galaxies represent a pivotal phase in the development of massive, quiescent galaxy bulges that formed rapidly in the early universe.

Recently discovered solar observations from Bolivia (5250 m above sea level) and Mexico (4600 m above sea level) uncovered evidence of extremely low-energy neutrons that appeared during the intense solar flare of November 7th, 2004. Utilizing a Monte Carlo simulation, it was determined that these neutrons originated from the decay of electron positron pairs rather than direct observations of high-energy particles. The absence of detected gamma rays below a certain threshold supports this conclusion. The observed neutron energies are consistent with the expectations of thermal electrons from solar flares, and the lack of observed neutrons at certain elevations can be attributed to the Earth's magnetic field intercepting the electrons.

In the study of rotating main-sequence stars with substantial surface rotation rates, there are unexpected variations in angular momentum that cannot be accounted for by standard models of differential rotation and core rotation. This study focuses on determining the underlying causes of increased angular momentum in spinning stars, with particular attention to whether it results from the consumption of exoplanets or alternative explanations related to angular momentum dynamics within the stars themselves. We employed a technique called the moment of inertia from spectroscopic surface velocities, which provided precise measurements of angular momentum in a group of rapidly rotating F-type stars. This method showed that the most spinning stars have significantly higher angular momentum than expected, with up to 37% arising from the moment of inertia rather than planetary consumption. This finding is further supported by models indicating that consumption of exoplanes would lead to increased contraction of the core and hence a higher moment of inertia than observed. As a result, we believe that other factors such as angular momentum generated through rotationally induced mixing in the core or related processes are more likely responsible for the observed variations in angular momentum.

Accurately identifying rumors is crucial in today's information-rich society, where false news can spread quickly. Since the emergence of new false news is constant and requires up-to-date knowledge, traditional machine learning models have significant limitations. These models rely on extensive training data and struggle with generalization, especially when faced with novel, unknown information. To address this challenge, we propose a novel approach called the Multimodal Meta False News Detector (MMFND), which utilizes both text and images. This model leverages metadata and small amounts of local, recently collected information to make predictions. MMFND consists of three key components: a neural process encoder, a shared neural process predictor, and an instance-specific predictor. These components work together to effectively handle partial, locally obtained information and contribute to the general knowledge pool. When faced with a new instance, the model combines world knowledge with local information to generate a rumormonger or not, with an confidence level. Experiments using our custom-built Multimodal Twitter False News Dataset (MTFND) show that our meta-model outperforms conventional machine learning models and our baseline expert system.

This research paper examines a one-dimensional transport equation featuring local extrema and non-convex flux. A comprehensive analysis of the equation's properties has been conducted, revealing that solutions with initial data in the space $H^1(\mathbb{R})$ exhibit smoothness for infinite time if the flux function is smooth and convex, but may develop singularities in a finite time if it is not. A primary goal of this study is to explore the behavior of solutions with singular points, culminating in an in-depth examination of a specific model equation whose solutions exhibit self-similar singularities.

Recently, Golay complementary sequences have gained significant attention due to their superior performance in multiple-access technologies. This research extends Golay complementary arrays to the next generation, introducing a new type of golay complementary arrays in polyphase form. A key characteristic of these arrays is that any two different elements from the set are complementary, offering advantages in multi-carrier systems. This document outlines the requirements for these arrays and provides a method for constructing a specific type of golay complementary array in quadriphase form. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that any golay complementary array in biphiase form can be modified to the quadriphase version.

Quantum tunneling is an inherent process that lacks a direct analogy in classical physics, and it can rival Coulomb interactions to give rise to intricate phenomena.
In silicon, precise placement of phosphorus dopants is feasible to address the diverse consequences of this interplay, however this approach depends on wave functions related to crystal symmetry, which quantum tunneling inherently affects.
In this study, we examine double donor molecules composed of two directly-placed phosphorus atoms, focusing on the valley interference that arises from their arrangement.
Valley interference allowed us to identify a valley-orbitating charge that swaps spin in a controlled manner, demonstrating the exchange of spin by displacing one of the donors to a distance of 0.7 nm ($\rm \pm 0.1$ nm).
This spin-swapping mechanism can be triggered by applying an electric field to displace the donors, which we found to result in an extremely narrow range of valley polarization, thus it may serve as a building block for quantum gates that exchange spin and valley properties.

Complex systems consisting of multiple interacting components typically follow nonlinear dynamics that are difficult to model using traditional methods. As a result, these models usually simplify the system's components and dynamics, which can lead to inaccurate predictions in unfamiliar situations. In contrast, our approach leverages only raw time-series data to train a graph neural network that automatically discovers the underlying dynamics and component interactions, without presuming a specific structure or model format. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in predicting various complex system attributes using only historical data, and show it can handle a wide range of systems, including non-linear ones, and even generate a meaningful graph of component interactions.

We introduce an infinite family of recursive formulas for calculating the number of distinct partitions that can be formed from successive applications of a specific homotopy theory operation, known as the smash product, combined with the partition function. By incorporating an extra variable in one formula, we derive an identifying characteristic, thereby providing a solution to a problem posed by D. G. Northcott. Another formula, derived from the Eulerian transformation, offers an alternative approach to calculating partition numbers. Furthermore, our methods yield explicit formulas for counting specific subclasses of partitions, thereby establishing connections to established results and renowned formulas, such as the generating function for distinguishing partitions and the isomorphism class counts derived from the symmetric group under equipartition.

A major challenge in creating highly realistic virtual patients is building an realistic simulated head injury. A novel approach to creating highly detailed synthetic head injury images has been proposed, utilizing a progressive adversarial variational auto-encoder. This model, called PA-VAE, consists of two main components: a variational auto-encoder (VAE) and a progressive adversarial network (GAN). The VAE component ensures the stability and smoothness of the generated data, while the GAN component ensures the synthetic data mimics real-world head injury images. To further enhance the simulation, PA-VAE was trained to generate intermediate features between fake and real data. The model was applied to simulate head injury images, rather than directly manipulating individual image features. Experimental results show that the proposed method successfully generates highly realistic synthetic head injury images, surpassing the quality of existing methods.

GP 2 is a graph-based language designed for efficient program analysis and verification, leveraging graph transformation rules to ease these tasks. However, achieving efficient execution requires significant development expertise and may impede the scalability of graph-based methods. In response to these limitations, we present the GP 2 Enhanced compiler, which incorporates multiple optimization techniques to accelerate program execution, specifically by utilizing a dynamic reordering of rules to achieve faster results, and including a refined memory management system to minimize memory usage. Additionally, the compiler offers a simplified interface for interfacing with external tools, including C and Java, via JNI and native interfaces respectively.

In contrast to conventional contrastive learning frameworks that separate modules for input projection and feature extraction, a unified structure is proposed that integrates both functions within a single module using dual branches. This combined module simultaneously produces two sets of features equidistant from the decision boundary, thereby indirectly determining the projective distance required for reducing the domain shift. Experimentally, this unified framework was found to outperform separate structures across 4 datasets, achieving a notable improvement of 3.38% in the median of the distribution of domain adaptation accuracy.

We have identified an infinite set of locally arc-transitive graphs whose automorphism groups act faithfully on vertex and edge colorings, specifically on a class of twisted wreath graphs constructed from a quartic graph and a group of order 2. Notably, this discovery exhausts the possible structures of locally transitive, vertex and edge 4-colorable graphs with an automorphism group that acts faithfully on both vertex and edge properties.

This study focuses on improving Group Lasso, particularly for models featuring categorical variables with a large number of dimensions. Presently, existing methods process such data by converting categorical variables to indicator matrices, but this causes poor performance due to the large size of these matrices in high-dimensional settings. Our approach introduces a novel penalized logistic regression Group Lasso method that handles categorical variables as unified numerical values. We then establish theoretical guarantees for the proposed algorithm and demonstrate its superior practical performance through simulated and real-world experiments involving large datasets.

Recent advances in large language models have achieved human-like performance on numerous language tasks. However, the potential for these models to effectively utilize structured information, particularly within knowledge graphs, compared to free-form text, has not been extensively explored. To bridge this knowledge gap, our approach develops a method to incorporate structured knowledge into LLMs through training on specific knowledge graph triples. We demonstrate that LLMs pre-trained with our technique outperform baseline models on tasks that leverage knowledge graphs. Specifically, our method shows comparable performance when compared to training models on corresponding natural language statements, and significantly improves performance when there is limited labeled training data available. Notably, our approach also yields comparable results to graph-specific models, often considered the gold standard.

Achieving a seamless visual experience and optimal system performance when displaying line joins on vector maps requires an efficient anti-aliasing technique. However, the limitations of OpenGL API hinder optimal rendering results when approximating the anti-aliased effect through multiple triangles. In an attempt to rectify this issue, this study introduces a straightforward yet high-quality method for directly generating anti-aliased polygons on the fly during rendering. Our proposed technique yields noticeable performance enhancements and a genuine anti-aliased effect, outperforming traditional triangulation methods. Furthermore, this technique is adaptable for rendering other complex shapes and can produce various high-quality polygon formats to meet the requirements of various applications.

In noisy environments, where speech is compromised and difficult to understand, speech enhancement technology can provide relief for individuals who are hearing impaired or need real-time transcription. Deep learning-based models have significantly improved speech enhancement performance but often require large amounts of data for training, making them less practical for being part of speech-enabled applications. A new Dual-Path Convolution Recurrent Network has been proposed to enhance single-channel audio in noisy environments. This new model combines two distinct modules: a convolution-based front-end that reduces noise levels and a recurrent-based back-end that refines the output. Exhaustive experiments on two separate audio enhancement tasks demonstrate the superiority of the proposed model, with results showing it outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in terms of objective and subjective evaluation metrics.

Recently introduced multi-fluid models hold promise in refining the simulation of atmospheric convection within weather and climate simulations. A dynamic framework by nature, this method eliminates several of the mass-flux convection scheme's assumptions that are no longer valid at modern model resolution levels. Nonetheless, the optimal approach for solving the multi-fluid equations in relation to atmospheric convection remains unknown.
