We derive one-step recurrence formulas for linear stochastic partial differential equations on the surface of a sphere, which involve random forcing, both in the case with minimal smoothness requirements and with added smoothness, leading to new convergence results for these equations forced by stationary random fields.

The flow of complex liquids is significantly influenced by surface tension and
crystalline ordering within the bulk. However, even when both factors are negligible,
 fluids like soap foams exhibit unexpected friction properties depending on their structural
 features, specifically the angle of their grains. A unified framework is introduced
 that explains how the granular structure impacts friction through gradient energy,
 applicable to a range of packings from random to highly ordered configurations.

This study presents an outlier-robust, skin-cancer image classification model using a two-tiered architecture. In the first section, a convolutional neural network called Residual Dense Network (RDNN) categorizes skin cancer images into melanoma and hypermelanosis. With an accuracy of 93.58%, this network demonstrates outstanding performance comparable to leading models, including EfficientNet and DenseNet. To detect tumor types, a second, separate classification is performed. In the second part, a support vector machine (SVM) is used to identify abnormal training images, relying on entropy calculations to separate outliers from regular samples. Our research indicates that, in comparison to the current benchmark, our model accurately classifies skin cancer images, while the SVM's ability to detect unusual samples or enhance model generalization remains promising areas for further exploration.

The interaction between a rotating fluid and a less dense, chemically distinct gas that undergoes a convective instability within a confined space is being studied in a Hele-Shaw cell. When the inner surface of the cell is kept stationary, various patterns of the interface between the fluids result from an initial perturbation, including steady-state configurations with multiple fingers. It has been observed that before the formation of a quasiperiodic fingering pattern caused by the cell's rotation, the interface is curved in a way that favors pattern stability. In addition, there is a minimum magnitude of cell rotation required to start the branching of a initially formed bubble, which marks the beginning of the fingering pattern. It has been found that this threshold can be explained by the Rayleigh--Benard instability of the interface between the fluids. When the inner surface of the cell is made to rotate smoothly, a variety of patterns of the interface between the fluids emerge, including patterns with multiple bubbles and branches, and patterns with asymmetric, transient shapes. Scientists have identified the presence of two specific isomers, 1-ethynyl-1-cyclopentadiene and 1-ethynyl-2-cyclopentadiene, of ethynyl cyclopentadiene (C5H5CCH) towards the TMC-1 direction using the ALMA telescope. Isomeric structures were confirmed through the non-equivalence of ethynyl and cyano group placements as indicated by SPITZER and GBT observations of 13C and 14N isotopic species of CN cycles, which show a ratio of (CCH)/((CCH)2) of 0.32±0.03, and a ratio of (CN)/((CN)2) of 0.53±0.04. Isotopic fractionation patterns indicate a chemical origin rather than optical effects, and the spatial distribution of ethynyl cyclopentadiene is consistent with that of cyclopentadiene. The column density of ethynyl cyclopentadiene was found to be 2.5×10^12 cm^-2, with ratios of cyclopentadiene to ethynyl cyclopentadiene of 2.3±0.3, similar to other PAHs in TMC-1.

In neural machine translation, the attention mechanism has been widely used to weigh input elements for output creation. However, research reveals that the attention mechanism can be flawed because it may concentrate solely on a single, misleading element while ignoring more precise information. This study proposes a novel attention mechanism, look-ahead focus, which examines the current state and predicts a weighting that rejects misleading elements. We test this new mechanism on several translation tasks and find it outperforms the standard attention mechanism. Furthermore, when combined with conventional attention, it yields comparable results and is simple to implement.

The widespread adoption of grid computing was significantly facilitated by a well-planned strategy to translate complex technical concepts into accessible language, thereby attracting a broader range of computer users. This paper delves into the world of grid computing during the early 2000s, a period characterized by rapid technological evolution, to explore how clear and simple explanations helped pave the way for this advancement. A detailed analysis of grid computing's development, culminating in the development of grid service-based architectures, is presented through the stories of key individuals and project leaders, offering first-hand accounts of this transformative period. The resulting framework provides valuable insights into the successful translation of grid computing, which can be applied to similar challenges in computer technology and related fields.

A novel model, called the Dissipative Unified Dark Substance model, has been developed which combines two similar cosmological theories, known as $f(R,G)$ and $f(Q,T)$, and allows for the interpretation of dark matter and energy's roles in the universe's evolution and expansion. The new model's characteristics were determined through the use of the variational method and conformal transformation techniques. Consequences of this new model were then assessed, starting with its effects on the universe's early stages, particularly during the Planck era, as well as in the universe's current state. Further investigation into the model's properties was conducted, accompanied by numerical analysis of its parameters.

This study explores the implications of the J/ψ particle decaying into invisible matter for light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter. The research examines the J/ψ decay's impact on neutrino oscillation experiments, specifically INO and Double Chooz, which rely on low-energy neutrinoless disappearance measurements. It also investigates the J/ψ decay's effect on dark matter models, specifically a scalar dark matter particle coupled with a Majoron neutrino, which would render the J/ψ invisible. The study utilizes the J/ψ invisible decay width to constrain light sterile neutrino masses and couplings with the heavy quarks, as well as the neutrino oscillation parameter sin²2θ, which affects the J/ψ invisible decay width. It also derives the J/ψ invisible branching ratio and decay width to facilitate future experiments that can detect this process. The research finds that a 10 times increase in J/ψ production at B-factories would significantly improve the sensitivity to light sterile neutrinos and couplings with the heavy quarks, but would not improve the sensitivity to the neutrino oscillation parameter sin²2θ. It also finds that the J/ψ invisible decay width constraints are already satisfied for the dark matter models examined, but the absence of forward jet and missing energy in the J/ψ decay modes (e.g. ψ(2S)) could provide a distinct signature for light sterile neutrinos. This study introduces multivariate functional singular spectrum analysis (MFSSA) across various dimensional domains, building on the foundations of multivariate singular spectrum analysis (MSSA). We offer a detailed explanation of the algorithm's components, including a numerical example and the R programming code to demonstrate the MFSSA process. Additionally, we conduct a simulation study to evaluate the performance of MFSSA in extracting relevant information and distinguishing between different dimensional domains. A real-data application involves analyzing multivariate functional time series in the context of economic growth across various countries, utilizing MFSSA to identify salient features and bridge the gap between time series and spectral domains.

The local time of a one-dimensional random walk is a measure that indicates the frequency of visits to a particular point. We have demonstrated that the squared local time, condensed to its relevant scale, converges to a well-defined random variable for a random walk that operates in an infinite time frame. Notably, if the walk is symmetric, this convergent variable is identical to the square of the absolute value of a specific Gaussian process, which is well-documented and referred to as the Gaussian free field. Our findings also extend to discrete time models.

The ICRF test facility IShTAR at the Max-Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in Germany features a plasma source with a linear plasma generator. This source produces plasma in helicon mode, similar to sources found in future devices such as the ITER plasma-surface interaction test facility. A discrete element method was employed to model the plasma source's electronics and fluid dynamics simulations were used to model plasma behavior. However, to ensure accuracy, it is crucial to validate the simulation against actual plasma source data. A study was conducted to verify the simulation in multiple areas, including plasma parameters, particle flux, and wall flux, across various plasma source configurations. It was discovered that increasing the plasma frequency in the source could lead to instability in plasma behavior. Additionally, a study was conducted to examine the plasma source's behavior in helicon mode, revealing that it can operate within a specific range of plasma frequencies that maintain plasma stability.

While gold-standard pathological diagnosis is highly reliable, it requires significant effort to perform tasks like identifying and counting individual cells. To streamline this process, a common approach involves using advanced nucleus segmentation technology. However, effectively training such models is complicated due to issues such as nuclei that are fused with each other, or with the surrounding tissue background. To address this challenge, researchers have been exploring methods of automatic nucleus segmentation based on point annotation, which involves marking the centres of individual cells rather than outlining each cell manually. Although these models show significant improvement over traditional methods, they often require large amounts of data for training, which can be difficult to obtain in the field of histopathology. In response to these challenges, the proposed W-Net architecture tackles the limited-data problem of nucleus identification in histopathology images, specifically in lung cancer specimens, using a limited amount of data. This happens as W-Net excels in pinpointing cell centres rather than outlining cells fully. As a result, even though there is enough information for diagnosis from the feature maps produced during this process, the model is still relatively small. To evaluate W-Net's performance, a new evaluation metric called the centre-based accuracy was created, which measures the similarity between annotated cells and identified cells based on their centres rather than outlines. In comparison with several other deep learning nucleus identification models, W-Net demonstrates superior performance in terms of data size and centre-based accuracy.

The local exchange theorem for certain conjugacy classes within the special orthogonal group SO_(2d+2) and the symplectic group Sp_(2d+2) has been proven by Bump and Ginzburg. However, their proof relies on characteristics not equal to two. In our research, we demonstrate the characteristics-two version of the local exchange theorem for the specified conjugacy classes within SO_(2d+2) and Sp_(2d+2). Additionally, we provide explicit formulas for the centralizer of an even semisimple class in both groups.

Graph convolutional neural networks, a key component of graph neural networks, are theoretically grounded in the graph signal processing domain, specifically in the realm of spectral convolutions. However, the practical feasibility of these methods is limited by the need for significant amounts of access to node data. In contrast, the usability of graph convolution is enhanced when using spatial convolutions, despite the lack of clear computational explanations. This study aims to bridge this gap by providing a simple frequency-domain analysis of graph convolution, leveraging matched filtering theory to facilitate an intuitive comprehension of the underlying mathematics. A new type of spectral convolution was discovered, referred to as the 'identity convolution', which can be used to understand the behavior of low-pass filters in the frequency domain. A new method of approximating these convolutions was also developed, which can be used to speed up the training of graph neural networks.

In a three-dimensional spacetime, Einstein's gravity theory is transformed to represent a scalar field with a self-attractive force. The field's equation can be reinterpreted using Chern-Simons theory, incorporating both the gravitational and gauge fields. The resulting theory yields static soliton and black hole solutions when the system's state does not change over time. However, when allowed to rotate, the system produces holonomic hairy black holes that grow and shrink in response to parameter variations, in addition to stationary soliton solutions. The entropy generation phenomenon associated with hairy black holes is observed when these solutions have specific winding numbers. The paper's appendix details the conformally related solutions to Einstein's gravity equipped with a cosmological constant.

Elastography, an advancing imaging technique, allows the non-invasive visualisation of tissue pathologies by identifying the physical properties of tissues. Accurate estimation of mechanical properties relies on precise measurement of elastogram displacement and strain in the lateral direction. However, significant sources of error hinder this estimation, particularly the limited view angle available in clinical practice. This study presents a novel virtual source synthetic aperture (VSSA) technique to enhance the estimation of mechanical properties in the lateral direction. By recreating the radiofrequency ultrasound data using virtual sources, the technique provides a more comprehensive 2D aperture, leading to improved frequency content, increased resolution, and a longer usable aperture length. Consequently, this results in the estimation of displacement and strain being less affected by limited view angle, allowing for accurate estimation in the lateral direction even in extreme scenarios. When compared to the conventional synthetic aperture technique and real-time elastography, the VSSA method demonstrates superior performance in both simulation and clinical scenarios.

Imperative algorithms and logical proofs in sequent calculus or natural deduction coexist as distinct yet related concepts. This interconnection suggests a fundamental equivalence, which we can express as the notion that imperative algorithms essentially embody a form of proofs with cut operations. This equivalence serves as the foundation for an expanded framework, which we call "logical pseudocodes." Each statement in logical pseudocodes is analogous to a step in natural deduction, ensuring correctness and safety in accordance with the original specifications. This approach can be seen as a natural extension to the concept of a computability logic web, but now incorporating the capacity for forward reasoning.

In the $k$-centers clustering problem, we aim to establish a set of clusters defined by hyperballs with the same radius, effectively dividing the input data into distinct groups based on geographical proximity. For data residing in a metric space of high dimensions, we have developed a one-shot algorithm for approximating this problem, resulting in a solution where the radius is nearly optimal and the number of clusters is nearly the optimal value. More specifically, for data in a high-dimensional space, our algorithm produces a clustering with a number of clusters and a radius, both of which compare favorably to the optimal solutions when considering the problem's inherent difficulty.

We introduce a novel hierarchical strategy for resolving large-scale discrete-state stochastic chase-evasion games on graphs, specifically those with complex layouts, by subdividing the graph into distinct regions that can be easily solved for at a local level. We then employ a straight-forward linear programming approach to determine optimal policies for these individual areas, and subsequently match these local solutions to obtain a cohesive global strategy. We prove the effectiveness and validity of this method by demonstrating its equivalence to a centralized optimal solution for the full graph. Furthermore, we show that this hierarchical method can yield significant performance improvements compared to flat solutions, as well as reduced computational requirements for large-scale problems.

To facilitate the evaluation of high-energy muon colliders, we have developed a modified "vector boson approximation" that accounts for the effects of both $W$ and $Z$ bosons in the $s$-channel. By leveraging a new, efficient numerical method for solving the $2\to 2$ scattering equation, we have derived precise expressions for the efficient vector boson approximation (EVVA) case. Furthermore, we have established guidelines for the validity of EVVA and investigated its limitations compared to the exact results. Our findings have been applied to a general process, such as Higgs production, and we have specifically evaluated the cross-sections for the $HWW$ and $HHVV$ processes that dominate the $WW$ and $ZZ$ pair productions, respectively. Our study indicates that, at 2 TeV muon colliders, the total $WW$ and $ZZ$ pair productions can be accurately represented by the $HVV$ process induced by $H$ boson decays, with an overall normalization of 2.85 times the SM prediction, with respect to the exact results obtained using the full $WW$/$ZZ$ matrix elements.

In multi-task reinforcement learning, efficiency can be significantly improved when agents learn multiple skills simultaneously. However, existing methods often fail when a new task causes existing knowledge to become severely impaired, a problem known as catastrophic interference. We discovered that in modular model-based multi-task reinforcement learning, newly acquired information is isolated from previous knowledge, thereby preventing interference. By dividing knowledge into distinct modules, we identified two types of interference: one affecting a module's underlying dynamics models and the other impacting the policy associated with a module. By modifying the policy and dynamics loss functions, we found that modules can be made refractory to interference, resulting in improved performance when learning new tasks. Through controlled and fully unsupervised experiments, we validated the efficacy of this approach, finding that modular reinforcement learning consistently performed better than a monolithic method control group.

We are presenting a concise report on the events that transpired during the 1964 International Congress of Logic, Philosophy, and History of Natural Science held in Leipzig, East Germany. This convention was notable for having a notable absence of Western logicians, which significantly influenced the meeting's atmosphere. Despite this challenge, the conference managed to succeed in its objectives, thanks in large part to the dedication and effort of its participants. A gathering of prominent logicians, including Kurt Godel, Alonzo Church, and Hilary Putnam, did not occur as the paper had initially predicted. However, the author did get the opportunity to meet with Stephen Kleene, who provided valuable insights into the historical development of logic systems.

This study confirms that for functions u, whose real and imaginary parts both belong to the Sobolev space H^3, the following inequality holds: if u is not identically zero and satisfies the Dirac equation in the unit ball B_1 in R^3, then there isn't a point x in R^3 \{0} for which |u(x)|/|x|³ ≤ 1 hold. Additionally, if there is a point x_0 in R^3 \{0} where |u(x_0)|/|x_0|³ = 1, then u is proportional to 1/|x_0|³ times the real or imaginary part of (a_1/a_2)∇(1/√a_2)), where a_1 and a_2 are the scalar and vector parts of the function u, and ∇ denotes the gradient operator.

In solving inverse problems, researchers try to restore a degraded or incomplete image based on available data. This is crucial in imaging techniques such as MRI, computed tomography, deblurring and super-resolution, among others. Because the inverse problems often involve reconstructing images that contain subtle details and richness, traditional methods that use single objective functions to drive optimization have been complemented by techniques based on generating realistic images. In particular, Conditional GANs have gained significant attention for solving such problems, though training these models is known to be challenging due to unstable training, low-quality generated results, and difficulty in designing appropriate architectures. To address these difficulties, we propose a novel regularized CGAN framework that incorporates two loss functions: a least-squares adversarial loss and an Laplacian regularization loss. This results in well-conditioned training, prevents the vanishing gradient issue, and allows for the capture of rich details in generated images. We evaluate the proposed method on several tasks, including image denoising, deblurring and super-resolution, showing its effectiveness in reconstructing high-quality images.

This study examines fractional dynamical systems from a symplectic perspective. We identify the necessary conditions for a system to possess invariant surfaces, which are determined by the system's parameters and the index of the system's differential operator. Specifically, we show that in two-dimensional spaces, all invariant surfaces exist if the system's operator index is one. However, in higher dimensional spaces, only certain components of the system's parameters ensure the existence of invariant surfaces. particularly, when the system's operator index is greater than one, no invariant surfaces exist except in exceptional cases. We further illustrate that certain fractional systems with one-dimensional surfaces can exhibit chaotic behavior depending on the system's parameters.

The interstellar medium is home to many regions that scatter pulsar radiation, yet these sources remain poorly characterized on a small scale. Pulsar scintillation, also known as "pulse to pulse" or "patchy" scintillation, occurs when the Earth moves the line of sight across the turbulent plasma within the interstellar medium, revealing patterns of scintillation that brighten and fade at specific frequencies. This study examines 617 hours of data from the Arecibo telescope observing the pulsar PSR B1133+16 at a frequency of 1.4 GHz, resulting in detailed maps of scintillation patterns that indicate the presence of multiple sources of turbulence in the line of sight. By modeling the observed patterns, it is possible to reconstruct the three-dimensional structure of the interstellar medium surrounding the pulsar, revealing several localized sources of turbulence that shape the scintillation patterns, and imply the presence of dense and ionized gas within a few parsecs of the solar system.

This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through expanded convolution neural networks (E-CNNs). WN achieves realistic waveform generation using extensive self-autoregression, but its lack of pitch controllability hinders its applications. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel method that ties the kernel size of E-CNNs to the pitch output from our pitch estimation model, effectively creating a periodic layer in the model. We further explore two model variations: a fully periodic model and a partially periodic model with only one transient E-CNN layer. Both models were evaluated on the LJS107K dataset, with the partially periodic model yielding a score of 3.83, the periodic model yielded a score of 3.56 on the test set.

Bicategories provide a framework for studying balanced equations. A key aspect of bicategories is the presence of balanced marks, which can be thought of as shadows of equations. These marks can be combined using bicategorical operations that mirror the equation's structure. A significant aspect of balanced marks is their ability to capture both local and global properties of equations. This property is crucial in establishing the connection between balanced marks and the fundamental group of a space, as it allows for the definition of conjugacy classes using shadows. This approach can also be found in the work of Moerdijk and Segal on low-dimensional topological quantum field theories.

In the game GMD:Geometric Hidden Markov Models, certain observations are artificially created and embedded into the hidden states, called "noises". Previous research has shown that noise states can be efficiently identified using dynamic programming techniques. By contrast, we identify an explicit difficulty in navigating GMD models, namely that noise states are consistently positioned at the periphery, never at the center, and always require a circumventive path to reach the observer. We call this challenge "the noise localization hardship". In our study, we extract a key aspect of this difficulty and apply it to a more minimalist setting, resulting in the creation of a new model category: Harsh Local Hidden Markov Models (HLHMMs). HLHMMs possess several distinctive features, including reversible paths and unobservable initial states. Notably, a notable sub-group of these models coincides with hidden versions of well-known linear time-invariant systems. We develop novel detection strategies for these models and conduct comprehensive performance assessments to demonstrate the effectiveness of our methods.

In recent years, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have been widely applied to complex network analysis, despite primarily being designed for static simple graphs. GNNs typically rely on a Euclidean distance metric that can lead to inaccurate results for many real-world datasets involving large distances. We propose a novel weighted convolution layer that leverages the Koszulian distance, a more suitable alternative for many applications, especially those involving a clear direction or hierarchy. Furthermore, we introduce a new category of GNNs, Lorentzian Graph Neural Networks (L-GNNs), incorporating the Koszulian distance, and demonstrate its effectiveness on high-stakes real-world data, including brain connectivity and stock market networks, achieving superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods.

This research focuses on the inverse problem of identifying damaged structures within a coupled acoustic and mechanical system, specifically with a focus on plate damage. An inversion method based on the element-free kriging algorithm is introduced to determine the parameters of a damage indicator function, which in turn indicates the extent and location of damage. Numerical simulations demonstrate the effectiveness of this inversion technique across various scenarios, including both 2D and 3D models and with point and extended damage types.

We present a novel exponential delay discounting model incorporating
variations in impulsivity, which is analogous to the 2007 Tsallis delay discounting
model proposed by Takahashi, with a dual nature allowing for the inclusion of
variations in impulsivity. This model's underlying mechanism is a non-equilibrium
thermodynamic hypothesis similar to that of the Tsallis distribution, which we
validate through an analysis of the model's parameters. A key finding is that the
impulsivity parameter's effect on present bias can be reversed, depending on the
degree of present bias, which is consistent with empirical observations. This model
can be seen as an dynamic and dual version of the Tsallis delay discounting
model, providing a possible explanation for the complex and sometimes counterintuitive
results obtained in related research.

We explore the connection between hefty gravity's harmonic gauge identities and their implications for general relativity's harmonic gauge. It is demonstrated that only a subset of hefty gravity's harmonic gauge identities are relevant, and these are shown to be equivalent to general relativity's harmonic gauge identity using the Einstein tensor. Furthermore, this specific identity is found to be associated with the conformally coupled sector of hefty gravity. Additionally, we investigate the conformally coupled sector of hefty gravity and its relation to massless gravity within the context of a specific, high symmetry scenario.

For a class of quadratic Hamiltonians, a transformation of Weyl-Wigner symbols through a change of variables reveals the canonical thermal equilibrium quantum states, using the Weyl-Wigner formalism in the phase space. A new set of operator conjugate variables is introduced to easily identify the Connes automorphisms driving the unitary canonical transformations of the Hamiltonian in thermal equilibrium, whose form is otherwise complex and not immediately apparent from the original variables. The new variables simplify the representation of the Hamiltonian's Connes automorphisms, exposing the explicit form of the unitary operator driving the canonical time evolution. The new perspective also highlights the distinct unitary operator transformations that lead to the same thermal equilibrium state, whose physical consequences differ by a multiple of the system's Planck constant. The transformation from the original variables reveals a new, non-obvious operator representation of the Hamiltonian, with Matlise involution determined by the Connes automorphism, whose matrix elements define the coupling between the harmonic oscillators in the quantum field. The complexity of the original variables necessitates the change of variables to demonstrate the emergence of the Fock space from a Hamiltonian with a simple quadratic form. The new perspective is applicable to a wide range of Hamiltonians, including those with periodic potentials, nonlinear interactions, and their variants, whose analysis was previously inaccessible with the original variables.

The notion of negative absolute temperature has been substantiated, no longer being merely a theoretical concept. Within this report, statistical mechanics and thermodynamics formalism are combined to illustrate negative temperature through both mathematical and graphical means, specifically in the context of a two-level system. We contend that the simplicity of these calculations can offer undergraduates a clear, tangible understanding of the concept of negative absolute temperature.

Within the framework of an easiest scoto-seesaw model, we generate a comprehensive understanding of type-II seesaw theory. This involves examining the neutrino sector's characteristics, as well as the phenomenology associated with dark matter composed of WIMPs and the stability of the Higgs vacuum. By incorporating dark matter, we obtain a relevant tree-level interaction between the dark sector and the standard one, which includes a neutral component of the Higgs doublet that contributes to the WIMP's mass. Furthermore, we identify a specific parameter range that meets both dark matter and neutrino sector requirements. Additionally, we determine that in the easiest scoto-seesaw model, the Higgs vacuum's stability is ensured for a minimum range of dark matter density parameters. Moreover, we determine the minimum range of dark matter density parameters necessary to prevent the Higgs vacuum from becoming unstable at the electroweak scale.

We employ exact diagonalization to examine the effects of spin-orbit coupling and electron-electron interactions on the $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ orbital levels in cubic transition metal oxides. By calculating magnetic properties and considering the overlap between $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ orbitals, we find that the $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ levels must be close to each other, with a minimum level spacing of approximately 0.6 electron volts. This requirement is met in 4d and 5d transition metal oxides with small charge transfer energy. In such cases, the oxides's physics is determined by the overlap between $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ orbitals rather than the distinction between them. Consequently, the $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ level structure can be simplified to a single band in 4d and 5d transition metal oxides with small charge transfer energy, allowing us to derive a hub-and-spoke band structure.

This study focuses on relative quantum geometries within the context of conformal field theory, specifically for certain types of boundary conditions associated with torus compactifications. We begin by outlining the principles of relative quantum geometry in chapter 2, highlighting the role of geometric operators, their measure, and associated topological invariants. Chapter 3 delves into the computation of torus topological invariants for both generic and semi-chiral boundary conditions via an analytical formula. Furthermore, we establish a direct relationship between these invariants and the coefficients of specific polynomial equations governing generic boundary conditions. Additionally, we investigate semi-chiral boundary conditions in detail, providing a comprehensive analysis of the associated geometric measures, roots of polynomial equations, and resulting topological invariants.

Using generative adversarial networks, a novel application in image editing has emerged, which could supplement medical diagnoses. By removing artifacts and anonymizing patient information, GANs can re-create authentic images from clinical data. Although this technique holds promise for enhancing image quality, its potential side effects on medical modeling tasks have yet to be explored. Our research involves using editing GANs to manipulate fake images, which mimic real images containing pathological information. Our primary findings reveal that, depending on the specific model employed, both stylebank and single-class editing GANs can lead to overfitting and poor generalization performance. In contrast, multi-class editing GANs demonstrate improved overall performance. To illustrate the practical uses of this technology, we edited fake images representing healthy patients, which were then used to train a model to classify real images featuring lung disease. Our data showed that this approach yields accurate results comparable to training the model using unedited fake images representing healthy patients.

ViDaExpert is an application for multidimensional data visualization and advanced analysis. It is capable of handling object-feature tables that include numerical values and text-based labels for objects and features. The tool enables users to embed their data in high-dimensional spaces using various techniques such as PCA, t-SNE, UMAP, and Autoencoders, and it supports both static and interactive visualizations to facilitate the understanding of complex data structures and patterns. With multiple assessment metrics and graphical representations, ViDaExpert simplifies the process of evaluating and selecting the most suitable dimensionality reduction technique for specific data analysis tasks.
